title: 10 tf transferred to the project as 10 kN: why GOST-compliant formatting does not fix the load
description: The force of 10 metric ton-force equals 98.0665 kN. We show the identified error in transferring the load and the change in the support check result.
seo_title: 10 tf and 10 kN in the project: load recalculation error
seo_description: The force of 10 metric ton-force equals 98.0665 kN. We show the identified error in transferring the load and the change in the support check result.
seo_keywords: ton-force to kilonewtons, 10 tf kN, load error project, acceptance of design documentation GOST
content:
In the original statement, the equipment reaction on the support equals 10 tf. In the design calculation, a line "10 kN" appeared, although the engineer claims the number was transferred unchanged and the documentation is formatted according to the adopted standard. The same digit does not mean the same load: ton-force and kilonewton differ by almost ten times. In such a case, the conversion of the quantity must be checked, not just the completion of the title block.

How a remark on formatting became a strength question

The conditional design assignment contains a requirement for documentation formatting and a separate initial statement from the manufacturer. For support O-2, the manufacturer indicated a force of 10 tf. The example directly confirms that this is metric ton-force, i.e. 1000 kilogram-force, not the mass of the unit and not the US short ton-force.

The designer transferred the digit 10 into a cell headed "kN" without conversion. Then he compared it with the limit force of 50 kN set for this check and drew a positive conclusion. The other circumstances of the calculation case are agreed: it is the same support, the same direction and the same force under consideration. The discrepancy cannot be explained by one party having used the mass of the whole unit and the other a separate reaction.

The contradiction has an established source. It arose at the transition from the statement to the calculation table. Correct document designation, a neat frame and the presence of a signature do not confirm the correctness of that transition. Acceptance of formatting and verification of the initial load remain different tasks.

Recalculation that changes the result

The reference value is 1 kgf = 9.80665 N. Therefore 1 metric ton-force equals 9806.65 N, or 9.80665 kN. For ten ton-force we get 98.0665 kN. The decimal comma here does not denote a thousands separator: it is an ordinary fractional value of a single force.

Now the comparison is performed in one unit: 98.0665 kN is greater than 50 kN. The previously recorded positive result for O-2 is not confirmed; the set limit is exceeded by about 48.07 kN. In the original erroneous table a completely different force of 10 kN was compared, so its margin of 40 kN has no relation to the task under consideration.

The primary NIST table gives the coefficient for kilogram-force. Through the explicitly established metric definition of ton-force our recalculation was obtained. In the same table there are other units with the English word ton, so the coefficient cannot be selected by a single similar name. The input unit of the example is established before the calculations.

Why tf cannot simply be replaced by tonnes

A tonne as a unit of mass and a ton-force as a unit of force denote different physical quantities. If the source actually contains mass, its conversion into a load would require a relevant calculation setup. In our case there is no such uncertainty: the manufacturer delivered precisely the force on O-2. There is no need to introduce repeated multiplication by acceleration after the conversion to newtons has already been performed.

Nor can 98.0665 kN be considered a newly measured load. It is the same specified initial parameter expressed in a different unit. Its reliability as a condition and the completeness of the model itself are considered separately. Correcting the unit does not replace the assessment of combinations, distribution over other supports or the actual condition of the structure.

A contractual reference to formatting rules does not establish a different conversion coefficient for physical units. Even if the package meets all agreed graphical requirements, a proven incorrect transfer of force remains a substantive remark. A dispute about which standard is indicated on the title page should not conceal the specific exceedance already found in the accepted task.

How to correct the calculation package

In the log of initial data, the original line "O-2: 10 tf" is retained and the applied correspondence "98.0665 kN" is indicated beside it. The calculation receives the corrected value with its source. Then the dependent conclusion and related documents in which the erroneous number 10 kN may have remained are reviewed. Changing only the cell heading is not enough if the underlying results have already been copied manually.

For checking the correction, the reverse operation is useful: 98.0665 kN corresponds to the same 10 tf. It will reveal an accidental repeated conversion. Rounding to 98.1 kN does not change the negative result relative to the conditional 50 kN; the choice of the number of digits should not be used to obtain a convenient margin.

A technical remark can be formulated without general criticism of the formatting: "The statement sets a force of 10 tf for O-2. In the calculation, 10 kN were used without conversion. With correct conversion, 98.0665 kN are obtained, exceeding the established criterion of 50 kN. The initial value and related results must be corrected." If such an error is found before acceptance of the project, send the materials to NPI "Nedra" for a substantive discussion of the calculation issue.
